title: Microkernel Oracle: lightweight runtime estimator for sequence-aware kernel hedging
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Goal: Build a lightweight "microkernel oracle" that predicts per-request relative performance across a candidate set of kernel implementations using a compact feature vector (seqlen profile, batch size, model shard layout, device memory headroom, recent latency tail). The oracle will be used as a low-cost hint to the existing scheduler to hedge kernel choices under tight latency SLOs and reduce expensive microbench probing during steady-state.
background: We currently rely on microbench probes and coarse profiling to choose kernels. Probing is accurate but adds jitter and doesn’t always generalize across mixed workloads. Heavy autotune jobs are costly to run in production for small tail improvements. The oracle aims to: (1) minimize online probing, (2) surface a ranked candidate list with confidence, and (3) gracefully degrade to safe defaults when uncertain.
design_notes: Oracle features: (a) single-request summary: total tokens, prefill tokens, decode tokens, max context window; (b) histograms: recent per-shard occupancy + seq-len quantiles; (c) device environment: free-memory fraction, concurrent-streams, GPU SM util snapshot; (d) model metadata: architecture family (e.g. transformer-blocks), quantization profile. Predictor: lightweight ensemble (logistic reg + tiny decision trees) trained on microbench labels (latency, p95, memory-fits). Decision output: ranked kernel IDs + confidence score + a small predicted cost delta. Safety: if confidence < threshold or predicted p95 > SLO margin then fallback to conservative kernel. Explore multi-armed bandit layer for continual adaptation with Thompson sampling capped by a regret budget per-hour.
acceptance_criteria: Oracle produces a ranked kernel list with confidence for >95% of requests in test workload
When used by scheduler, end-to-end p95 latency on mixed production-like workload is <= baseline p95 + 3% while reducing microbench probes by >= 60%
Oracle hot-start from historical fingerprints reduces cold-probe frequency for new traffic shards by >= 40%
No increase in out-of-memory incidents attributable to oracle-driven choices during canary (0 incidents across 72h canary)
implementation_plan: Phase 1: Offline dataset collection — augment existing microbench runs with compact request fingerprints and environment snapshots (2w)
Phase 2: Train & evaluate lightweight predictors on cluster of archived traces; pick candidate model family and quantization (1w)
Phase 3: Integrate predictor as a sidecar service in runtime with gRPC hint API and a Proto-lite fingerprint (1w)
Phase 4: Canary rollout on non-critical tenant pool with shadowing of kernel choices for 72h, collect telemetry (1w)
Phase 5: Enable hedging policy: when oracle confidence high, schedule recommended kernel; when low, probe at reduced rate with bandit control (2w)
Phase 6: Monitor, iterate thresholds, and expand rollout (ongoing)
metrics_to_track: regret_from_oracle_choices (measured as extra latency vs best-observed)
experiment_notes: Initial offline experiments show that a 3-feature decision tree (seqlen-bin, batch-size, free_mem_pct) recovers the best kernel 78% of the time on our validation set across Llama2 variants. Adding tiny ensemble boosted to 86% while keeping inference cost < 50us per prediction on CPU. Bandit controller simulated with historical traffic yielded 22% fewer p95 spikes vs static policy in stress tests.
rollout_plan: Canary on 'dev-inference-pool' (no SLAs) with shadow mode for first 72h
If canary metrics pass acceptance criteria, enable hedging for 10% of 'beta' pool traffic for 1 week
Expand to 50% of beta pool after threshold checks, gradually increase to production clusters with rollback windows
Maintain shadow logging for 30 days post-rollout for drift analysis
